title: Path Traversal and File Upload Security
description: Learn how path traversal attacks let users read files outside intended directories, and how insecure file uploads can turn your server into a malware host. Explore path validation, file type restrictions, and safe storage patterns in .NET.

data.text: Path traversal and insecure file uploads are two sides of the same problem: trusting user input to define file paths or file contents. A path traversal vulnerability lets an attacker read or write files outside the intended directory by using special characters like `../` to climb up the folder tree. Insecure file uploads let an attacker upload a web shell or malware that the server later executes.

Path traversal happens when an application uses user input to construct a file path without proper validation. On Windows and Unix-like systems, `../` moves up one directory. An attacker who requests `../../../../etc/passwd` from a file-serving endpoint might escape the web root and read sensitive system files. Double encoding, null bytes, and Unicode normalization can bypass naive filters.

terms.definition: An attack that uses special path sequences like ../ to access files outside the intended directory.
A malicious script uploaded to a server that gives the attacker remote command execution through the web server.
Checks performed before storing an uploaded file, including type, size, content, and name validation.

data.title: Vulnerable file-serving endpoint
data.content: This C# endpoint reads a file based on user input without validating the path.

data.title: Never trust filenames or paths from users
data.text: Path traversal is not just a .NET issue — it affects every platform. The fix is to resolve the final path and verify it starts with the expected base directory. If the resolved path escapes the base directory, reject the request immediately.

The correct approach is to resolve the full path using `Path.GetFullPath` and then verify that the result starts with the expected base directory. This handles `../` sequences, double encoding, and symbolic links. Even better, avoid taking user input as a filename entirely — use a database ID to look up the file path on the server.

data.title: Safe path resolution
data.content: Resolve the path and verify it stays within the uploads directory.

data.text: File uploads require multiple layers of defense. First, validate the file extension against an explicit allowlist. Second, inspect the file content (magic bytes) to confirm the file type matches the extension. Third, store uploads outside the web root or on a dedicated storage service like Azure Blob Storage. Fourth, generate a new random filename on the server instead of trusting the original name.

data.title: Secure file upload in .NET
data.content: Validate the extension, inspect the content, and store with a random name.

data.text: Client-side validation improves the user experience but cannot be trusted for security. An attacker can bypass JavaScript restrictions by crafting raw HTTP requests with curl or Burp Suite. Always enforce the same validation rules on the server. The browser also sends the original filename in the `Content-Disposition` header of multipart uploads, which is why the server must rename the file.

data.title: React file upload form
data.content: The form accepts a file and posts it to the API. Server-side validation is the real security gate.

data.title: Path traversal and file upload checklist

items.text: Resolve file paths and verify they stay inside the intended directory.
items.hint: Use Path.GetFullPath and check the result starts with the base path.

items.text: Use database IDs instead of filenames when serving files.
items.hint: This eliminates path traversal entirely because the server controls the path mapping.

items.text: Allowlist file extensions and validate magic bytes.
items.hint: A .exe renamed to .jpg must still be rejected by content inspection.

items.text: Store uploads outside the web root or on dedicated blob storage.
items.hint: Azure Blob Storage, S3, or a directory with no execute permission.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Path traversal uses ../ sequences to escape intended directories and access sensitive files.
Always resolve paths with GetFullPath and verify the result is inside the base directory.
File uploads need extension allowlisting, content validation, safe storage, and server-generated names.
Client-side validation is a usability feature, not a security control.
data.takeaway: Trust no path or filename from the client. Resolve, validate, and regenerate names on the server.
